title: General solutions of trig equations
keywords: n pi plus one n alpha
examples: When we find the general solution, what does the 'n' represent?
If the period is pi, how does that change the general solution format?
Can you show me an example where the coefficient of n is not one?

explain.say: Today we learn about general solutions for trig equations. These solutions describe all possible angles that make the equation true. We use a variable like 'n' to represent any whole number.

draw.text: General Solutions: n is any integer

explain.say: Some equations have solutions that repeat regularly. This repeating pattern is called periodicity. We write the general solution using the form n pi plus one n alpha. This covers all possible angles.
Consider the equation sin theta equals one divided by two. The basic solutions are pi plus one n and three pi minus one n. We combine these into one general form.
Another example is cos theta equals one divided by two. The solutions are pi plus 2n and negative pi plus 2n. We can write this more simply as n pi plus one n pi.

Imagine you are looking at the sun's path across the sky. It follows a repeating cycle every day. This daily pattern is like the periodicity we are learning today. The general solution helps us predict when it will happen again.

faq.q: What does 'n' stand for in the general solution?
faq.a: The letter n stands for any integer. This means n can be any whole number, positive or negative, including zero.
asks: What is the value of n?
Does n have to be a positive number?

faq.q: Why do we use the form n pi plus one n alpha?
faq.a: This specific form helps us write down all possible solutions in a compact way. It accounts for the periodic nature of the trigonometric functions.

faq.q: If the period is two pi, is the general solution always 2n pi?
faq.a: Not always. The general solution depends on the specific function and the value it equals. Two pi is just one possible period.
asks: How do I find the period?
Is 2n pi the only general solution for sin theta = 0?

faq.q: What if the equation involves tan theta?
faq.a: For tangent, the general solution is usually simpler. It often takes the form n pi plus alpha, because the period of tan is pi.
asks: Is the general solution for tan always n pi?
Does tan follow the same rules as sin or cos?

faq.q: Can I use two different general solutions for the same problem?
faq.a: Yes, sometimes. Different forms might look different but describe the exact same set of angles. You must check which form is simplest.
asks: Are there multiple ways to write this?

facts: Trigonometric functions are periodic, meaning their values repeat at regular intervals.
The general solution represents every possible angle that satisfies the given equation.
For sine and cosine, the period is two pi radians.
The general solution often involves an integer variable, typically denoted by n.

quiz.say: What is the general solution for cos theta equal to one divided by two?

options.show: n pi plus one n pi
options.say: n pi plus one n pi

quiz.why: The cosine function repeats every two pi, and the solutions pi/3 and 5pi/3 are separated by two pi. Combining them gives the pattern n pi plus one n pi.

wrong.0: This only gives solutions when theta is zero or two pi, missing the other required angles.
wrong.1: This only accounts for one set of solutions and misses the symmetry around the circle.
wrong.2: Adding 2pi does not change the set of solutions, so this is redundant and incorrect.

quiz.say: Find the general solution for tan theta equal to one divided by three.
quiz.why: The tangent function has a period of pi. Therefore, the general solution is simply the principal value plus integer multiples of pi.

wrong.0: This incorrectly doubles the required angle increment.
wrong.2: This assumes the angle is pi/3, which is not the correct principal value for tan theta equals one divided by three.
wrong.3: Using two pi suggests the period is two pi, but the period of tangent is pi.

quiz.say: If sin theta equals zero, what is the general solution?
quiz.why: Sine is zero at zero radians and pi radians. These solutions are separated by pi, so the general form is simply n pi.

wrong.0: This shifts the solutions up by pi/2, which is incorrect for sine being zero.
wrong.1: Adding pi to n pi does not change the set of solutions and is needlessly complex.
wrong.3: This only gives solutions at zero and two pi, missing pi, three pi, etc.
